issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident in a combat pilot, the threat profile should more plausibly center on accident recurrence, mechanical failure, bodily vulnerability, or generalized hypervigilance. 'Watching others closely for signs that they might harm me' implies an interpersonal assault/paranoia-like threat that is not supported by the trauma type or by the other selected items.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal set otherwise reflects post-traumatic identity disruption and emotional numbing ('Lost Emotions', 'Identity Loss'). 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is comparatively more characteristic of interpersonal violation or severe dissociation/depersonalization. In this profile it sits awkwardly with the accident trauma and with the other appraisal items, reducing thematic coherence of the node.

vignette:
At 54, Mikaere had spent most of his adult life in the cockpit, a combat pilot known among his peers for discipline, precision, and a habit of always knowing where the exits were. That habit had once been part of the job; after the accident it became something he felt he had to do everywhere. He was of Oceanic background, married, and still living in the same home he shared with his wife, yet the life he inhabited after the trauma felt markedly narrower than the one he had known before. The accident had been life-threatening and sudden, the kind of event that left no time to think in orderly terms. He described a moment of catastrophic danger in which survival had depended on reacting instantly, and he recalled the visceral certainty that he might not make it out alive. Even now, when he spoke about it, he returned to the physical details of confinement, danger, and the need to find a way out. It was not just that the event had been frightening; it had taught him, in a way that felt absolute to him, that danger could arrive without warning and that being unprepared was intolerable.

In the weeks that followed, Mikaere found himself scanning spaces before he could settle in them. In restaurants, waiting rooms, and even when entering a room in his own house, he would automatically identify doors, windows, and possible exits before allowing himself to sit. He was embarrassed by how reflexive this had become, but he also felt unable to ignore it. At home, where he had once expected to relax, he remained on guard. He noticed sounds in the night with unusual intensity, and if he heard movement elsewhere in the house he was alert immediately, as though part of him were still stationed for danger. He described himself as “superalert” and said that even inside familiar walls he did not feel fully at ease. The vigilance was not limited to dramatic moments; it settled into everyday life, shaping how he moved through ordinary spaces and how quickly he could let his attention soften.

Mikaere’s work as a combat pilot made the changes especially hard to hide. Flying had always required close attention, but after the accident he found himself taking in every detail of the environment before he could feel even a little comfortable. He would check access points, think ahead to how he would leave a place, and keep his body keyed to movement around him. What had once been confidence in operational readiness now felt to him like a persistent need to stay ahead of danger. He did not describe panic so much as an unrelenting watchfulness, a sense that he could never fully stand down. Over time, this left him feeling separate from the version of himself he remembered from before the accident. He said he felt as if he no longer knew himself anymore, and that this unfamiliarity was one of the most disturbing parts of the aftermath. The man who had once seen himself as composed and capable now felt altered in ways he could not fully name.

What troubled Mikaere most was not only the danger he still sensed around him, but the changes he believed had happened inside him. He told the therapist that he was certain he had permanently changed for the worse. The words carried a heaviness that seemed to come from his own experience of being unable to return to the emotional life he once took for granted. He said, with a flatness that suggested resignation, that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. This was not a passing worry for him; it had become part of how he understood himself. He had begun to regard his emotional life as damaged, as if the accident had taken something essential and left him with a reduced or altered version of who he had been. He could still function, still work, still fulfill obligations, but he did so with the conviction that some inner quality had been lost.

By the time he sought help, these changes had been present for long enough to affect both his sense of ease and his relationships at home. His wife had noticed that he was always checking the house, always alert to sounds and movements, and always orienting himself to exits whenever they went somewhere together. Mikaere himself was weary of the constant scanning, weary of feeling so unlike himself, and increasingly worried that this was simply who he had become. He came for help not because he believed the memory of the accident had faded, but because it had not: it remained lodged in the way he moved through the world and in the conclusions he had drawn about his own permanence. What he hoped for, though he could barely imagine it, was some way to feel safe enough to stop looking for the door at every turn, and some reassurance that the man he had been was not gone for good.
